The provisions for equipment removal are unavoidable as they will also need to be utilized for the initial construction of the OTEC plant. One possible exception is that the evaporators may be able to be installed initially through the penetration on the top of the lower hull section where the intake screens will eventually be installed. However, after deployment, this area will be submerged and no longer provide “dry” access to the evaporators. 17 OESI 2.0 M-1 T-1-P1.1 – Objective 3 Report April 2025 4.3 Additional Platform Coupling Considerations for Add-On Designs Planned integration of an OTEC plant with a new oil and gas platform would be advantageous because the design can build upon the vast history of innovation and success in the hurricane-prone GOA for oil and gas facilities. The expertise and experience is available within oil and gas platform/hull design companies as well as the USCG to make a robust design to minimize the risk of storm damage. In addition, offshore facility design companies have the knowledge of existing platform design considerations including buoyancy, stability, mooring, and collision avoidance systems to avoid conflicts with key platform components. The main considerations in locating an OTEC plant must be resilience to predominant wind and sea conditions, crane location, lifeboat location and deployment pathways, emergency egress, communication, lighting, confined space procedures, and equipment layout considerations. Further, if an add-on OTEC is to be connected to an existing platform, the installation of underwater supports will be more technically challenging due to the need to perform underwater welding. Underwater welding is a specialized skill that requires special equipment, available skilled welders, as well as suitable weather. These challenges would add costs and limit the construction window for implementation. 4.4 Working Fluid Selection and Assumptions The significant HSE considerations for refrigerant (or working fluid) selection are described in the Objective 2 report. However, the performance of the two fluids was not addressed. A robust evaluation of the heat transfer performance comparing the two fluids has not been done as that requires more sophisticated heat exchanger modelling such as that done by heat exchanger manufacturers. As outlined in the Objective 2 report, this study evaluated OTEC performance using two working fluids: ammonia and R134a. Both have advantages and drawbacks in terms of their use, cost, availability, safety, environmental impacts, and so on. In the case of the hull-integrated OTEC plant, the original heat exchanger performance was based on R134a, and in the add-on cases, the refrigerant used in the original heat exchanger performance was ammonia. The heat exchanger expected performance obtained from vendor information for these fluids is also documented in the Objective 2 report. A simplifying assumption was made regarding the performance for other fluids in order to provide equal net power.
